title: The Years You're Rushing Past Are the Golden Years Here's a Simple Way to Enjoy Them
author: Michael Foster
summary: Foster observes that the busiest, most difficult years of parenthood—when money is tight, time is scarce, and demands feel overwhelming—are often among life's golden years, though parents rarely appreciate them in the moment. He argues that the regret many older adults feel stems from failing to savor what was directly in front of them, and offers a practical antidote: intentionally learning what your children care about most, then meeting them there and taking pleasure in their joy. The simple discipline of setting a phone reminder to ask one child about their passion and listen deeply can recalibrate a parent's gaze toward the preciousness of ordinary moments before they vanish.
points: The stretched-thin years of early parenthood contain blessings most parents don't recognize until they're gone—the regret of grandparents shows what missed presence costs.
Parental joy comes not from solving all problems but from learning to take real pleasure in someone else's enjoyment, a quiet art of fatherhood worth cultivating.
A single mechanical discipline—setting a phone alarm to ask one child about their passion—can crack open presence and transform ordinary conversations into golden memories.
Regret in middle age often surfaces as the realization you didn't fully appreciate what was right in front of you while raising young children.
quotes: The most difficult, stressful years of your life, the years when you're buried under little kids, trying to buy a house, scrambling for resources, climbing the ladder at work, the years when there's never enough time and you're running around like a chicken with its head cut off… those years, believe it or not, are some of your golden years. Some of your best memories will come from there.

I've heard a lot of people in their 20s and 30s talk about how mediocre their parents were, but how great they are as grandparents. A lot of that comes from regret. It's the realization that you didn't really enjoy what was right in front of you.

One thing I started doing was rehearsing in my head the things my kids care about, the things they love. I try to meet them there. I try to connect with them along those lines. And then, as simple as it sounds, I try to enjoy them enjoying things.
There are little doors into their lives. Some of their responses will be golden memories you treasure for the rest of your life.
That's one of the quiet arts of fatherhood: learning to take real pleasure in someone else's joy.

Here's a practical tip. Set an alarm on your phone that says, "Ask one of my kids about their thing or their day. Then listen and ask follow-up questions."” Archived from We Made People (Foster Substack) on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
